question: What starts and controls aircraft electrical circuits?

options.text: Switches and relays
Capacitors and inductors
Fuses and circuit breakers
Voltage regulators alone

explanation: Circuits are initiated and controlled by switches, operated by the crew or by the system, and by relays, which let a small current switch a larger one. Fuses and breakers protect circuits; they do not control them in normal use.

question: Where is the toggle switch most common?

options.text: Only in landing gear position sensing
In modern glass cockpits, replacing switch lights
Only inside fire detection loops
In older aircraft, as a general-purpose switch

explanation: The toggle switch is a general-purpose lever switch with isolating contacts inside, typical of older flight decks. Modern aircraft mostly use switch lights instead.

question: A multi-position toggle switch that springs back to the centre is operated by:

options.text: Turning it clockwise until it clicks
Pressing it twice to cancel the selection
Pressing and holding it in the direction wanted
Moving it once, after which it latches in place

explanation: A sprung-to-centre toggle returns to its central (often off) position when released, so it must be pushed and held in the desired direction for as long as the action is needed.

question: A simple two-position toggle switch has the positions:

options.text: Guarded and unguarded
On and off
Make and hold
Momentary and alternate

explanation: The basic toggle switch is simply on or off. Momentary and alternate action describe switch lights.

question: What does a switch light combine?

options.text: A push-action switch and an indicator light
A circuit breaker and a warning horn
A toggle switch and a fuse
A relay and a time delay

explanation: A switch light is pressed to operate, and its lens lights up to show the selected state or to warn that the switch needs selecting. Switch lights have largely replaced toggle switches on modern flight decks.

question: How does a momentary-action switch light work?

options.text: It switches off automatically after 30 seconds
It stays on until the circuit breaker trips
It is active only while held pressed
It latches on with one press and off with the next

explanation: Momentary action means press and hold to activate, release to deactivate. The latching behaviour is alternate action.

question: How does an alternate-action switch light work?

options.text: Pull out to activate; push in to deactivate
Press once to test the lamp only
Press and hold to activate; release to deactivate
Press and release to activate; press again to deactivate

explanation: An alternate-action switch light toggles: one press and release turns the function on, a second press and release turns it off. Press-and-hold is momentary action.

question: What can the light in a switch-light lens show?

options.text: Only that the circuit breaker has tripped
The selected state, or a warning that it should be selected
The voltage on the associated bus
Only that the switch has lost power

explanation: The indicator confirms the position that has been selected, or warns the crew that the switch needs to be selected. It does not show bus voltage.

question: Why are some switches fitted with a guard?

options.text: To prevent inadvertent operation
To make the switch easier to find in the dark
To protect the switch from moisture
To limit the current through the switch

explanation: A guard must be lifted before the switch can be moved, so critical functions cannot be operated by accident. Toggle switches and switch lights can both be guarded.

question: Which switch would typically be guarded?

options.text: The cockpit dome light switch
The fuel dump master switch
The panel lighting dimmer
The cabin reading light switch

explanation: Guards are fitted to switches whose accidental use would matter, such as fuel dump or generator disconnect. Lighting switches are not normally guarded.

question: Why is a generator disconnect switch guarded?

options.text: It is used only on the ground by engineers
It must be operated with gloves on
Its accidental use would have serious, lasting effect
It carries too much current to be left exposed

explanation: Disconnecting a generator is a significant action, often not reversible in flight, so its switch is guarded to stop it being operated by mistake.

question: What does the name "microswitch" refer to?

options.text: The microscopic size of its contacts
The small current the switch can carry
The very short time the switch stays closed
The small movement between make and break

explanation: The name describes the very small travel of the operating plunger between the make and break positions.

question: What is a microswitch typically used for in an aircraft?

options.text: Converting DC into AC for instruments
Regulating generator output voltage
Protecting a circuit against overcurrent
Detecting the position of a device, such as a door

explanation: Microswitches sense position, for example whether a door is open or closed, and can drive a flight deck indication or relays for a sequence. Circuit protection is the job of fuses and breakers.

question: On modern aircraft microswitches have largely been replaced by:

options.text: Centrifugal switches
Toggle switches
Proximity detectors
Bimetallic switches

explanation: Proximity detectors sense position without physical contact and are sealed, so they are more reliable than microswitches and have largely replaced them, for example on landing gear.

question: What makes a bimetallic switch operate?

options.text: A set temperature being reached
A set speed being reached
A nearby metal target
A set time having passed

explanation: A bimetallic switch is a thermal switch: it changes state when a certain temperature is reached. Speed is the centrifugal switch's trigger and time the time switch's.

question: Which is a typical use of a bimetallic (thermal) switch?

options.text: A landing gear downlock sensor
A battery overheat warning
An APU intake door timer
A starter motor cut-out

explanation: Thermal switches are used in fire detection, battery overheat and oil temperature warnings. A starter cut-out is centrifugal and a downlock sensor is usually a proximity detector.

question: What is a proximity detector?

options.text: A switch operated by a lever touching the target
A sensor that responds to the presence of a material
A switch that opens when a set temperature is reached
A relay that closes after a set delay

explanation: A proximity detector senses that a material is near and uses that response to work a switch, relay or transistor. It does not need to be touched.

question: What are the three main types of proximity detector?

options.text: Inductive, capacitive and magnetic
Resistive, thermal and optical
Thermal, centrifugal and timed
Toggle, guarded and alternate

explanation: The major types are inductive, capacitive and magnetic. Thermal, centrifugal and time switches are separate kinds of switch.

question: Which type of proximity detector can sense non-metallic materials?

options.text: Inductive
Magnetic, provided the target is moving
Capacitive
Magnetic

explanation: Inductive and magnetic sensors need a metal target, but a capacitive sensor responds to any material, metal or not, liquid or solid.

question: An inductive proximity detector works because:

options.text: Its contacts are closed by the target pressing on them
Its temperature rises when the target comes near
Its capacitance changes when any material comes near
Its coil's inductance changes near a steel target

explanation: The sensor contains an inductance coil; bringing a ferromagnetic target close changes the coil's inductance, which the electronics read as "target near".

question: Which type of proximity detector replaces microswitches in landing gear systems?

options.text: Inductive
Centrifugal
Capacitive
Bimetallic

explanation: Landing gear position is commonly sensed by inductive proximity switches, each with a sensor on the gear structure and a metal target next to it.

question: A landing gear proximity switch consists of a sensor, a target and:

options.text: A capacitor in the flight deck indicator
A printed circuit card
A spring-loaded lever touching the target
A bimetallic strip in the sensor head unit

explanation: Each proximity switch has three parts: a printed circuit card in the landing gear accessory unit, a sensor on the gear structure, and a target (actuator) next to the sensor.

question: Why is a proximity switch unaffected by atmospheric conditions?

options.text: It is mounted inside the pressurised cabin
It is heated to keep moisture out
It is sealed and nothing touches it
It works only when the gear is retracted

explanation: The sensor is a sealed unit actuated by the target's presence, not by contact, so dirt, ice and moisture do not affect it and it is highly reliable.

question: A capacitive proximity detector senses a target because:

options.text: Its resistance changes with temperature
Its coil's inductance changes with a steel target
A moving magnet induces an EMF in its coil
Its capacitance changes near the material

explanation: The capacitive sensor detects the change in capacitance caused by material close to it. Inductance change is the inductive type and an induced EMF is the magnetic type.

question: Which proximity detector could monitor the fluid level in a hydraulic reservoir?

options.text: Magnetic
Capacitive
Centrifugal
Inductive

explanation: Because it can sense liquids as well as solids, ferrous or not, the capacitive detector can report high or low levels in hydraulic or fuel systems.

question: On what principle does a magnetic proximity detector work?

options.text: A temperature change alters a resistance
A change of capacitance alters a frequency
A changing flux induces an EMF in a coil
A target closes a pair of contacts

explanation: A coil in a magnetic field has an EMF induced in it whenever the flux changes. A moving ferrous object near the magnet changes the flux and produces a pulse in the coil.

question: What decides the size of the EMF induced in a magnetic proximity detector?

options.text: The colour of the target material
The temperature of the coil
The total amount of flux in the magnet
The rate of change of flux

explanation: Induced EMF depends on how fast the flux changes, so a faster-moving target gives a larger pulse. A steady flux, however strong, induces nothing.

question: A magnetic detector sits close to a rotating steel gear wheel. What is the frequency of its output?

options.text: The rate at which teeth pass the detector
The rotation rate of the wheel in revolutions per minute
The aircraft's AC supply frequency
Twice the rate at which teeth pass

explanation: Each tooth acts as a ferrous object and produces one pulse as it passes, so the output frequency equals the frequency of passage of the teeth. This is how the detector measures rotational speed.

question: What does a magnetic detector produce when several ferrous objects move past it?

options.text: A train of pulses
No output unless the objects stop
A single pulse only
A steady DC voltage

explanation: Each object changes the flux as it passes, so a row of objects, such as gear teeth, induces a train of pulses in the coil.

question: Which proximity detectors need the monitored material to be metal?

options.text: Capacitive only
Inductive and capacitive
Inductive and magnetic
Capacitive and magnetic

explanation: Inductive and magnetic sensors rely on a ferromagnetic or metal target. Only the capacitive type also detects non-metals.

question: What does a time switch do?

options.text: Operates a circuit when a metal target comes near
Operates a circuit when a set RPM is reached
Operates a circuit when a set temperature is reached
Operates a circuit after a set time has passed

explanation: A time switch or relay, started electrically or mechanically, activates a circuit once a specific interval has elapsed. Temperature, RPM and proximity are other switches' triggers.

question: Which is an example of a time switch in use?

options.text: A gear downlock sensed by a metal target
An APU intake door closing after shutdown
A starter motor cutting out at a set RPM
A battery overheat light at a set temperature

explanation: Closing the APU air intake door a fixed time (for example 30 seconds) after the APU shuts down is a time-switch function. The other examples are centrifugal, thermal and proximity switches.

question: How can a time switch be initiated?

options.text: Electrically or mechanically
Only by a rise in temperature
Only by the crew pressing a switch light
Only by a change in RPM

explanation: Time switches and relays can be started either electrically or mechanically; after the set interval they operate their circuit.

question: What operates a centrifugal switch?

options.text: A set interval of time having passed
A set temperature being reached
The RPM of a device passing a set value
A metal target moving close to it

explanation: A centrifugal switch activates or deactivates a circuit as the speed of a device increases or decreases through a preset value.

question: Which is a typical use of a centrifugal switch?

options.text: An oil temperature warning
A starter motor cut-out
A door position sensor
A fire detection loop

explanation: As the engine accelerates, the centrifugal switch cuts out the starter motor at a set RPM. Fire and oil temperature warnings use thermal switches, door sensing uses micro or proximity switches.
